topics.topic: Post-start symlink-refusal requirements for SQLite database and journal files
questions: Does a database or journal symbolic link introduced after startup remain permitted to SQLite, or must the kernel detect it and refuse the operation?
Does the symbolic-link refusal invariant apply to a database or journal link introduced after startup, or are SQLite-opened files exempt after the startup check?
Does the formal symlink-refusal invariant exclude SQLite-managed files after startup, or must SQLite database and journal symlink substitution also be detected and refused?

quotes: The database file and its journal are opened by SQLite, which Python cannot ask to refuse a link; the start's check covers them, and the kernel does not watch them after it: in a private directory only the kernel's user or root can place a link, and either can change any record directly, so a link gives them nothing more (owner, 2026-10-18).
judgement.why: The normative exception permits SQLite-managed database and journal links to go undetected after startup, while the unconditional formal invariant requires every symlink inside the data directory to be refused.

topics.topic: Handling of `..` during secure component-by-component path traversal
questions: When the component-by-component opener encounters `..`, must it reject the path or traverse to the parent directory?
Is `..` allowed and opened normally relative to the current directory descriptor, normalized before traversal, or refused?

quotes: Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's `O_NOFOLLOW` — a directory on the way with `O_PATH` as well, so a directory the kernel's user may only pass through is passed; empty and `.` components are skipped; the host is Linux (A20 rule 3), so no code asks whether a flag exists and there is no mode without it —, and the checks and the read use that one opened file, so the file checked is the file read.

A credential is resolved only when a request to its service is built: its secret file is read then, without following a symbolic link, and must be a regular file owned by the kernel's user with no permission for group or others; its content decoded as UTF-8, without one trailing newline, is the value.
judgement.divergence: One implementer refuses any path containing `..`; another opens `..` relative to the current directory descriptor and may read a configuration or credential outside the intended subtree. The installer notices whether startup succeeds, and the owner or contacted service notices whether the credential-backed request succeeds.
judgement.why: The component-walking rule explicitly handles empty and `.` components but leaves the security-relevant behavior of `..` unspecified.

topics.topic: Scope of the SQLite file exception and permitted journal and temporary-file modes
questions: Which SQLite-opened files are covered by the exception, and is SQLite required to use a particular journal and temporary-file mode?
Exactly which SQLite-opened files are exempt from the component-by-component `O_NOFOLLOW` rule, and which SQLite journal and temporary-file modes may the release use?

quotes: The data directory holds one SQLite database with every kernel record, a content-addressed area of value bytes and file fixtures named by digest, and the run spool, one subdirectory per run.

Every file the store opens itself is opened relative to the data directory it holds open from the start, each component with Linux's `O_NOFOLLOW`, never first asking whether the flag exists (A20 rule 3); a link met so later makes that store call fail with nothing written.

The database file and its journal are opened by SQLite, which Python cannot ask to refuse a link; the start's check covers them, and the kernel does not watch them after it: in a private directory only the kernel's user or root can place a link, and either can change any record directly, so a link gives them nothing more (owner, 2026-10-18).

Value bytes and spooled files are written to a temporary file, flushed, checked against their digest and size, and then renamed into place; a completed file a record names is never overwritten — a spooled file no record names, left by a change that failed, is replaced at its position.

On start, temporary files, value bytes no record names (left by a failed call, K-10; owner, 2026-10-07) and the spool directories of runs that ended and do not keep their spool (A14) are removed; nothing else is.
judgement.divergence: One implementer uses rollback journaling and treats only the main database and rollback journal as SQLite-managed exceptions; another uses WAL or temporary databases and exempts WAL, shared-memory and other SQLite auxiliary files as well. The owner or operator notices different files, locking and recovery behavior, and store operations may either accept or refuse auxiliary-file symlink substitutions.
judgement.why: The text neither defines what counts as SQLite's journal nor selects a journal or temporary-file mode, leaving observable persistence and refusal behavior to the implementer.

topics.topic: Minimum Linux compatibility baseline and behavior when required capabilities are unavailable
questions: What minimum Linux kernel, filesystem and Python-build capabilities are required, and what must happen when a nominally Linux host rejects or lacks the required open flags or semantics?

topics.topic: Opening requirements and readability assumptions for intermediate data-directory components
questions: Must intermediate directories under the data directory also be opened with `O_PATH`, and therefore permit traversal of an execute-only directory, or may the store require them to be readable?
Must startup deterministically refuse a non-Linux host, must packaging prevent execution there, or is arbitrary failure or execution permitted?

topics.topic: Required location and enforcement of configuration and credential files relative to the data directory
questions: Must the kernel enforce that the configuration and secret files are outside the data directory, is this an installer obligation that is not checked, or may such files be inside it?
